# sbsampling: Sequence-Based Spatially Balanced Sampling on the Sphere <a href="https://inbo.github.io/sbsampling"><img src="man/figures/logo.png" align="right" height="139" alt="sbsampling website" /></a>

[Van Calster, Hans](mailto:hans.vancalster%40inbo.be)[^aut]

[^aut]: author

**keywords**:  H3; GRTS; spatially balanced sampling; Sobol sequence

<!-- description: start -->
Implements spatially balanced sampling algorithms on the sphere using sequence-based randomization. It offers both continuous sampling from vector polygon geodata utilizing Owen-scrambled Sobol sequences, and discrete spatial sampling via the H3 global grid system. Both approaches operate natively on spherical geographic coordinates, eliminating the need for map projections while ensuring spatially well-distributed survey points.
<!-- description: end -->

The `sbsampling` package implements sequence-based spatially balanced sampling designs where the input sampling frame is in spherical coordinates (typically a vector polygon or multi-polygon).
The functions either directly sample from the continuous spatial domain or leverage the [H3](https://h3geo.org/) discrete global grid system for indexing spatial data into a hexagonal grid.

For sampling from the [H3](https://h3geo.org/) discrete global grid system, the package provides spatially balanced sampling via an adaptation of the Generalized Random Tessellation Stratified (GRTS) algorithm.
For a given random seed and H3 resolution, all sampling units are deterministically sorted such that consecutively ordered sampling units are spatially balanced samples for a given area on earth, which makes it suitable for so-called master sampling applications.

For direct sampling from continuous spatial domains without discretization, several implementations are provided.
One, is a modification of the balanced acceptance sampling (BAS) algorithm (Robertson) whereby points are drawn from a 2-D Owen-scrambled Sobol sequence and accepted when inside the sampling frame.
Its domain of applicability should be restricted to relatively compact spatial domains.
It is suitable for so-called master sampling applications.
For non-compact spatial domains, the package provides alternatives that directly route or warp the 2-D Owen-scrambled Sobol sequence inside a polygon without rejection sampling.

The implementations are written in [`Rust`](https://rust-lang.org/) and wrapped into an R package using [`rextendr`](https://extendr.rs/rextendr/).
The package is developed with the aid of large language models Google Gemini and Anthropic Claude Sonnet.
R code is kept to a bare minimum and the package has zero R dependencies.
All algorithms are thoroughly tested, both with unit testing and simulations.
The implementation is lightweight, cross-platform, fast and memory friendly.

## Installation

Install the development version from [GitHub](https://github.com/) with:

``` r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_git("https://github.com/inbo/sbsampling")
```

## Sampling algorithms

`sample_sobol()` is the main function for sampling from a continuous spatial domain.
`grts_h3()` is for sampling from a discretised spatial domain.

| Function | Domain | Rejection | Prefix stable | Master sample across polygons | Output |
|:---------|:-------|:----------|:--------------|:------------------------------|:-------|
| `sample_sobol(algorithm = "acceptance")` | Compact polygons | Yes, `rank` has gaps | Yes | Yes, with a shared `master_bbox` and `seed` | Sobol points |
| `sample_sobol(algorithm = "warp")` | Any, including sparse or narrow polygons | No | Yes | No | Redistributed Sobol points, warped into the polygon |
| `sample_sobol(algorithm = "routing")` | Any, including sparse or narrow polygons | No | Yes | No | Redistributed Sobol points ordered along the polygon's area |
| `grts_h3()` | Polygons, discretised to H3 cells at a chosen resolution | No | Yes | Yes, for a given `seed` and `resolution` | H3 cells with inclusion probabilities |

In short:

- If your polygon fills a reasonable share of its bounding box, use `"acceptance"`.
  It is the only continuous variant that can be used for master sampling: with the same `master_bbox` and `seed`, overlapping polygons share the same points in their overlap.
- If your polygon is sparse or narrow relative to its bounding box, use `"warp"`.
  It never rejects points and deforms the 2-D point pattern as little as possible (see the plots below).
- `"routing"` is the continuous analogue of GRTS: it orders points along the exact area of the polygon, so that consecutive ranks are spatially balanced along that 1-D ordering.
  It displaces points much more than `"warp"` does, so we recommend it only if you specifically want this GRTS-style ordering.
- Use `grts_h3()` if you need a discrete sampling frame (cells), design-based estimation with explicit inclusion probabilities, or a master sample that is consistent across study areas on the H3 grid.
  The sort key of a cell only depends on the cell and the seed, so a cell has the same sort key in every study area.

`"warp"` and `"routing"` depend on the exact area of the polygon that is being sampled.
Their samples are therefore **not** consistent across overlapping but differently shaped polygons.
For a master sample, use `"acceptance"` or `grts_h3()`.

### Limitations

- Input geometries must be `POLYGON` or `MULTIPOLYGON` in an angular coordinate system such as WGS84 (EPSG:4326) (geodetic CRS), converted to well-known binary (WKB).
- Polygons crossing the antimeridian (180°/-180°) must be split first, e.g. with `sf::st_wrap_dateline()`.

## Examples

### Sample from a continuous spatial domain

As an example spatial domain (sampling frame) from which we want to draw a spatially balanced sample, we extract Ashe county from the North Carolina state dataset that ships with the `sf` package.

We need to convert the geometries to well-known binary format to be able to use them as input for `sbsampling::sample_sobol()`.
We also extract and convert the bounding box geometry to illustrate the different ways in which the algorithms handle the Owen-scrambled Sobol sequences that are generated in the bounding box.

```{r ashe-county}
library(sbsampling)
nc_path <- system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf")
ashe <- sf::st_read(
  nc_path,
  quiet = TRUE,
  query = "SELECT * FROM nc WHERE NAME='Ashe'"
)
ashe_wkb <- ashe |>
  sf::st_geometry() |>
  sf::st_as_binary()
ashe_wkb <- ashe_wkb[[1]]
ashe_bbox <- ashe |>
  sf::st_bbox() |>
  sf::st_as_sfc()
ashe_bbox_wkb <- ashe_bbox |>
  sf::st_as_binary()
ashe_bbox_wkb <- ashe_bbox_wkb[[1]]
```

Drawing a sample using one of the Sobol sequence-based sampling algorithms, then proceeds as follows:

```{r example-sobol}
bas_sample <- sample_sobol(
  wkb = ashe_wkb, n = 20, seed = 456, algorithm = "acceptance"
)
bas_sample_sf <- sf::st_as_sf(bas_sample, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4267)
routed_sample <- sample_sobol(
  wkb = ashe_wkb, n = 20, seed = 456, algorithm = "routing"
)
warped_sample <- sample_sobol(
  wkb = ashe_wkb, n = 20, seed = 456, algorithm = "warp"
)
routed_sample_sf <- sf::st_as_sf(
  routed_sample, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4267
)
warped_sample_sf <- sf::st_as_sf(
  warped_sample, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4267
)
bbox_sample <- sample_sobol(
  wkb = ashe_bbox_wkb,
  n = max(bas_sample$rank) + 1,
  seed = 456,
  algorithm = "acceptance"
)
bbox_sample_sf <- sf::st_as_sf(
  bbox_sample, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4267
)
```

In case of the "acceptance" algorithm, a plot of the sample from Ashe county combined with the sample where we used the bounding box as input geometry (with same seed) shows that the returned `rank` has gaps: points are drawn in the bounding box and only those inside the polygon are accepted (darkgreen points are accepted, darkred points are rejected).

```{r plot-bas, echo=FALSE}
op <- par(xpd = TRUE)
plot(ashe_bbox, col = "grey")
plot(ashe$`_ogr_geometry_`, add = TRUE, col = "white")
plot(bbox_sample_sf$geometry, add = TRUE, pch = ".", cex = 5, col = "darkred")
plot(bas_sample_sf$geometry, add = TRUE, pch = ".", cex = 5, col = "darkgreen")
coords <- sf::st_coordinates(bas_sample_sf)
coords_bbox <- sf::st_coordinates(bbox_sample_sf)
text(
  x = coords_bbox[, 1], 
  y = coords_bbox[, 2], 
  labels = bbox_sample_sf$rank, 
  pos = 3,
  cex = 0.8,
  col = "darkred"
)
text(
  x = coords[, 1], 
  y = coords[, 2], 
  labels = bas_sample_sf$rank, 
  pos = 3,
  cex = 0.8,
  col = "darkgreen"
)
title("accepted / rejected")
legend(
  "bottomright", legend = c("accepted", "rejected"), pch = 15,
  col = c("darkgreen", "darkred"), bty = "n", cex = 0.8
)
par(op)
```

Alternatively, instead of rejecting points, we can apply exact area-warping or -routing on the Owen scrambled Sobol-sequence to redistribute the points directly inside Ashe county.
The `rank` now has no gaps because the algorithms map the sequence directly inside the geometry's exact area.
The redistribution of the points is much less severe in case of the "warp" algorithm as can be seen by the lines in the plot which connect the original position of the points when drawn from the bounding box geometry with the position after applying either exact-area warping or exact-area routing.
Routing treats the sequence as a 1-D ordering along the polygon’s area, so neighbouring ranks can end up far apart; warp stretches the 2-D point pattern to fit the polygon, so it keeps the 2-D spacing much better.


```{r plot-warp-rout, echo=FALSE}
bbox_sample_sf_20 <- bbox_sample_sf[bbox_sample_sf$rank < 20, ]

bbox_to_warped_df <- merge(
  as.data.frame(bbox_sample_sf_20), 
  as.data.frame(warped_sample_sf), 
  by = "rank", 
  suffixes = c("_start", "_end")
)

bbox_to_warped_sfc <- sf::st_sfc(
  lapply(seq_len(nrow(bbox_to_warped_df)), function(i) {
    coords <- rbind(
      sf::st_coordinates(bbox_to_warped_df$geometry_start[i]),
      sf::st_coordinates(bbox_to_warped_df$geometry_end[i])
    )
    sf::st_linestring(coords)
  }),
  crs = sf::st_crs(bbox_sample_sf_20)
)

bbox_to_warped_sf <- sf::st_sf(
  rank = bbox_to_warped_df$rank,
  geometry = bbox_to_warped_sfc
)

bbox_to_routed_df <- merge(
  as.data.frame(bbox_sample_sf_20), 
  as.data.frame(routed_sample_sf), 
  by = "rank", 
  suffixes = c("_start", "_end")
)

bbox_to_routed_sfc <- sf::st_sfc(
  lapply(seq_len(nrow(bbox_to_routed_df)), function(i) {
    coords <- rbind(
      sf::st_coordinates(bbox_to_routed_df$geometry_start[i]),
      sf::st_coordinates(bbox_to_routed_df$geometry_end[i])
    )
    sf::st_linestring(coords)
  }),
  crs = sf::st_crs(bbox_sample_sf_20)
)

bbox_to_routed_sf <- sf::st_sf(
  rank = bbox_to_routed_df$rank,
  geometry = bbox_to_routed_sfc
)

op <- par(xpd = TRUE)
plot(ashe_bbox, col = "grey")
plot(ashe$`_ogr_geometry_`, add = TRUE, col = "white")
plot(warped_sample_sf$geometry, pch = 22, cex = 0.5, add = TRUE, bg = "black")
plot(bbox_to_warped_sf$geometry, add = TRUE)
coords <- sf::st_coordinates(warped_sample_sf)
text(
  x = coords[, 1], 
  y = coords[, 2], 
  labels = warped_sample_sf$rank, 
  pos = 3,
  cex = 0.8
)
title(
  "warped",
  sub = "lines: position in the bounding box sample -> redistributed position",
  cex.sub = 0.7
)
plot(ashe_bbox, col = "grey")
plot(ashe$`_ogr_geometry_`, add = TRUE, col = "white")
plot(routed_sample_sf$geometry, pch = 22, cex = 0.5, add = TRUE, bg = "black")
plot(bbox_to_routed_sf$geometry, add = TRUE)
coords <- sf::st_coordinates(routed_sample_sf)
text(
  x = coords[, 1], 
  y = coords[, 2], 
  labels = routed_sample_sf$rank, 
  pos = 3,
  cex = 0.8
)
title(
  "routed",
  sub = "lines: position in the bounding box sample -> redistributed position",
  cex.sub = 0.7
)
par(op)
```

All Sobol-sequence algorithm variants result in the same sample in case we use the bounding box geometry as input:

```{r}
bbox_sample_acceptance <- sample_sobol(
  wkb = ashe_bbox_wkb,
  n = 20,
  seed = 456,
  algorithm = "acceptance"
)
bbox_sample_warp <- sample_sobol(
  wkb = ashe_bbox_wkb,
  n = 20,
  seed = 456,
  algorithm = "warp"
)
bbox_sample_routing <- sample_sobol(
  wkb = ashe_bbox_wkb,
  n = 20,
  seed = 456,
  algorithm = "routing"
)

all.equal(
  bbox_sample_acceptance,
  bbox_sample_warp,
  check.attributes = FALSE
)
all.equal(
  bbox_sample_acceptance,
  bbox_sample_routing,
  check.attributes = FALSE
)
```

The "acceptance", "warp" and "routing" algorithms are prefix stable: a sample of size `n` consists of the first `n` rows of any larger sample drawn with the same seed from the same polygon.
This allows you to extend a sample later (e.g. to replace unreachable sites) without changing the points that were already selected.

```{r prefix-sobol}
warped_10 <- sample_sobol(
  wkb = ashe_wkb, n = 10, seed = 456, algorithm = "warp"
)
all.equal(
  warped_10[, c("lon", "lat")],
  warped_sample[1:10, c("lon", "lat")]
)
```

```{r plot-prefix-sobol, echo=FALSE}
first_10 <- warped_sample_sf$rank < 10
plot(ashe$`_ogr_geometry_`)
plot(warped_sample_sf$geometry[first_10], add = TRUE, pch = 19,
     col = "darkgreen")
plot(warped_sample_sf$geometry[!first_10], add = TRUE, pch = 1,
     col = "darkgreen")
legend(
  "bottomright", legend = c("first 10", "next 10"), pch = c(19, 1),
  col = "darkgreen", bty = "n", cex = 0.8
)
title("prefix stability (warp)")
```

Both the first 10 points and the full 20 points are spatially balanced.

Only "acceptance" has the master sample property in addition to the prefix stability, provided that a common bounding box is used.
We can show this by adding a neighbouring county.
A sample of size 20 from Ashe county shares points with a sample of size 20 from the union of the counties.

```{r plot-acceptance-master-property}
asal <- sf::st_read(
  nc_path,
  quiet = TRUE,
  query = "SELECT * FROM nc WHERE NAME IN ('Ashe', 'Alleghany')"
)
asal_bbox <- asal |>
  sf::st_geometry() |>
  sf::st_union() |>
  sf::st_bbox()
asal_union_wkb <- asal |>
  sf::st_geometry() |>
  sf::st_union() |>
  sf::st_as_binary()
asal_union_wkb <- asal_union_wkb[[1]]

sample_ashe_within_asal_bbox <- sample_sobol(
  wkb = ashe_wkb,
  n = 20,
  seed = 456,
  master_bbox = asal_bbox,
  algorithm = "acceptance"
) |>
  sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4267)

sample_asal_within_asal_bbox <- sample_sobol(
  wkb = asal_union_wkb,
  n = 20,
  seed = 456,
  master_bbox = asal_bbox,
  algorithm = "acceptance"
) |>
  sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4267)

plot(asal$`_ogr_geometry_`)
plot(sample_ashe_within_asal_bbox$geometry, pch = 22, bg = "white", add = TRUE)
plot(sample_asal_within_asal_bbox$geometry, pch = 21, add = TRUE, cex = 0.7,
     bg = "black")
```


### Sample from the H3 discrete global grid system

We draw a spatially balanced sample with the aid of `grts_h3()` at resolution 7 of the [H3 resolutions](https://h3geo.org/docs/core-library/restable/) system.
This corresponds to hexagonal areas of approximately 5.16 km².
The `h3o` package can be used to, among other things, obtain the hexagon centroid or vertices.

The rows of the result are returned in GRTS order, i.e. by ascending `effective_key`: any first `k` rows are themselves a spatially balanced sample of size `k` with the same seed.
You can therefore draw a larger `n` than you need and use the sample sequentially, or extend a sample later without changing the cells already selected.

The `area_correction` argument controls the inclusion probabilities.
H3 hexagons do not all have the same area: their area varies by up to a factor of about 1.9 across the globe because of the icosahedral projection.
With `area_correction = FALSE` (the default), all cells have the same inclusion probability `n / N`, with `N` the number of cells covering the study area.
With `area_correction = TRUE`, sequential Poisson sampling is applied so that the inclusion probability is proportional to cell area.
In both cases, the result contains the `area_m2` and `ip` columns, and the number of cells `N` and the total area as attributes (`n_cells` and `sum_area_m2`), which are needed for design-based estimators.
For a per-area measurement `y` taken in the sampled cells, the Hájek estimator of the mean is `sum(y * area_m2 / ip) / sum(area_m2 / ip)`.

```{r example-h3}
h3_sample <- grts_h3(
  wkb = ashe_wkb,
  n = 20,
  resolution = 7,
  containment = "centroid",
  seed = 123,
  area_correction = FALSE
)
h3_sample$geom_points <- h3_sample$cell |>
  h3o::h3_from_strings() |>
  h3o::h3_to_points()
h3_sample$geom_hexagons <- h3_sample$cell |>
  h3o::h3_from_strings() |> 
  h3o::h3_to_vertexes() |>
  sf::st_cast("POLYGON")
```

We can visualise the selected spatially balanced sample and the H3 cells:

```{r plot-example-h3}
ashe_cells <- h3o::sfc_to_cells(
  ashe$`_ogr_geometry_`,
  resolution = 7,
  containment = "centroid"
)
ashe_hexagons <- h3o::h3_to_vertexes(ashe_cells[[1]]) |>
  sf::st_cast("POLYGON")
plot(ashe$`_ogr_geometry_`)
plot(ashe_hexagons, add = TRUE)
plot(h3_sample$geom_hexagons, col = "lightgreen", add = TRUE)
plot(h3_sample$geom_hexagons[1:10], col = "darkgreen", add = TRUE)
plot(h3_sample$geom_points, add = TRUE, cex = 0.3)
legend(
  "bottomright", legend = c("first 10", "next 10"), pch = 15,
  col = c("darkgreen", "lightgreen"), bty = "n", cex = 0.8
)
```

Drawing a smaller sample with the same seed yields the first rows of the larger sample:

```{r prefix-h3}
h3_sample_10 <- grts_h3(
  wkb = ashe_wkb,
  n = 10,
  resolution = 7,
  containment = "centroid",
  seed = 123
)
all.equal(h3_sample_10$cell, h3_sample$cell[1:10])
```

If you draw many samples from the same study area (e.g. in simulations), the tessellation can be computed once with `h3_get_coverage()` and passed to `grts_h3()` via the `cells` argument:

```{r h3-cells}
ashe_coverage <- h3_get_coverage(
  wkb = ashe_wkb, resolution = 7, containment = "centroid"
)
h3_sample_cells <- grts_h3(cells = ashe_coverage, n = 20, seed = 123)
all.equal(h3_sample$cell, h3_sample_cells$cell)
```
